accessible_name: Integer equivalence is an equivalence relation
listen_text: Proposition. Integer equivalence is an equivalence relation.
long_description: Proposition asserting reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity of the relation used to construct the integers.
name: prop
source_block:
\begin{prop} $\Intequiv$ is an equivalence relation.
\end{prop}

accessible_name: Definition of the integers as equivalence classes
listen_text: Definition. The integers are the equivalence classes, under integer equivalence, of ordered pairs of natural numbers. Equivalently, the integers are the quotient of the natural-number pairs by integer equivalence.
long_description: Defines the integers as equivalence classes of natural-number pairs under integer equivalence.
name: defn

accessible_name: Definitions of integer-class addition, multiplication, and order
listen_text: Display. three definitions on integer-equivalence classes. Their sum is the class with first coordinate a plus c and second coordinate b plus d. Their product is the class with first coordinate a times c plus b times d and second coordinate a times d plus b times c. The class of a comma b is at most the class of c comma d if and only if a plus d is at most b plus c.
long_description: Three aligned definitions on integer-equivalence classes.
name: align*

accessible_name: Natural-number embedding laws for integers
listen_text: Display. three embedding laws: the integer embedding of m plus n equals the sum of the integer embeddings of m and n; the integer embedding of m times n equals their embedded product; and m is at most n if and only if embedded m is at most embedded n.
long_description: Three aligned laws showing preservation of addition, multiplication, and order.
name: align*

accessible_name: Integer-embedding multiplication calculation
listen_text: Display. four-line calculation for multiplication under the integer embedding. The integer embedding of m times n is the class with coordinates m times n and zero; by the class-product definition this is the class with first coordinate m times n plus zero times zero and second coordinate m times zero plus zero times n; this is the product of the classes of m comma zero and n comma zero; therefore it equals embedded m times embedded n.
long_description: Four aligned equalities proving preservation of multiplication.
name: align*
source_block:
\begin{align*}
%		(m + n)_\Int  = \equivrep{m + n, 0}{\Intequiv} = \equivrep{m + n, 0 + 0}{\Intequiv} = \equivrep{m, 0}{\Intequiv} + \equivrep{n, 0}{\Intequiv} = m_\Int + n_\Int\\
		(m \times n)_\Int  &= \equivrep{m \times n, 0}{\Intequiv} \\
		&= \equivrep{m \times n + 0 \times 0, m \times 0 + 0 \times n}{\Intequiv} \\
		&= \equivrep{m, 0}{\Intequiv} \times \equivrep{n, 0}{\Intequiv} \\
		&= m_\Int \times n_\Int
	\end{align*}

accessible_name: Definition of the rationals as equivalence classes
listen_text: Definition. The rationals are the equivalence classes, under rational equivalence, of pairs of integers whose second element is nonzero. Equivalently, the rationals are the quotient of the Cartesian product of the integers with the nonzero integers by rational equivalence.
long_description: Defines rationals as rational-equivalence classes of integer pairs whose second coordinate is nonzero.
name: defn

accessible_name: Definitions of rational-class addition, multiplication, and order
listen_text: Display. definitions of rational-class arithmetic and order. The sum of the classes a comma b and c comma d is the class with numerator a times d plus b times c and denominator b times d. Their product is the class with numerator a times c and denominator b times d. For order, the first class is at most the second exactly when their difference is represented by a nonnegative integer numerator i and positive integer denominator j.
long_description: Aligned rational-equivalence-class operations plus the nonnegative-difference order clause.
name: align*

listen_text: Unsolved exercise. For all integers i and j, prove that the rational embedding preserves addition, multiplication, and the less-than-or-equal order.

accessible_name: The square root of two is irrational
listen_text: Theorem. The square root of two is not rational; that is, the square root of two is not an element of the rational numbers.
long_description: Theorem stating that the positive square root of two is not a rational number.
name: thm

accessible_name: Overlapping-squares proof diagram
listen_text: Diagram for the geometric irrationality proof. A large outer square has side m. Two equal inner squares, each of side n, occupy the lower-left and upper-right corners and overlap in a central orange square. Two congruent corner regions remain uncovered. Because m squared equals twice n squared, the central overlap has the same total area as the two uncovered regions. Calling the overlap side p and each uncovered-square side q yields p squared equals twice q squared, with p less than m and q less than n.
long_description: Two equal squares of side n overlap inside a larger square of side m. The central orange overlap and two uncovered corner squares encode a smaller solution to the same square-area equation.
name: tikzpicture

accessible_name: Definition of a Dedekind cut
listen_text: Definition of a cut. A cut alpha is a nonempty proper initial segment of the rational numbers with no greatest element. In detail: alpha is nonempty and is a proper subset of the rationals; whenever rational p is less than rational q and q belongs to alpha, p also belongs to alpha; and for every p in alpha there is a q in alpha with p less than q. The real numbers are defined to be the set of all cuts.
long_description: A cut is a nonempty proper initial segment of the rationals with no greatest element.
name: defn
source_block:
\begin{defn}[Cut] 
A \emph{cut} $\alpha$ is any non-empty proper
initial segment of the rationals with no greatest element. That is,
$\alpha$ is a cut iff:
\begin{enumerate}
	\item \emph{non-empty, proper}: $\emptyset \neq \alpha \subsetneq \Rat$
	\item \emph{initial}: for all $p,q \in \Rat$: if $p < q \in \alpha$ then $p \in \alpha$
	\item \emph{no maximum}: for all $p \in \alpha$ there is a $q \in \alpha$ such that $p < q$ 
\end{enumerate} 
Then $\Real$ is the set of cuts. 
\end{defn}

accessible_name: Order on Dedekind cuts
listen_text: Display. alpha is at most beta if and only if alpha is a subset of beta.
long_description: The cut order is defined by set inclusion.
name: align*

accessible_name: Completeness of the set of cuts
listen_text: Theorem. The set of cuts has the Completeness Property: every nonempty set of cuts with an upper bound has a least upper bound.
long_description: Theorem asserting that every nonempty bounded set of cuts has a least upper bound.
name: thm

accessible_name: Addition and nonnegative multiplication of cuts
listen_text: Display. two operations on nonnegative cuts. Alpha plus beta is the set of p plus q for p in alpha and q in beta. Alpha times beta is the union of the real-zero cut with all products p times q for nonnegative p in alpha and nonnegative q in beta.
long_description: Aligned set-builder definitions for adding cuts and multiplying nonnegative cuts.
name: align*
source_block:
\begin{align*}
	\alpha + \beta &= \Setabs{p + q}{p \in \alpha \land q \in \beta}\\
%	\alpha - \beta &\defis \Setabs{p - q}{p \in \alpha \land q \in \Rat \setminus \beta}\\
	\alpha \times \beta &= 
	\Setabs{p \times q}{0 \leq p \in \alpha \land 0 \leq q \in \beta} \cup 0^\mathbb{R} & \text{if }\alpha, \beta \geq 0_\Real
%	\alpha \div \beta &\defis 
%	\Setabs{\nicefrac{p}{q}}{p \in \alpha \land q \in \Rat \setminus \beta}  & \text{if }\alpha \geq 0_\Real, \beta > 0_\Real
\end{align*}

accessible_name: Additive inverse of a cut
listen_text: Display. negative alpha is the set of all p minus q such that p is negative and q is not in alpha.
long_description: Set-builder definition of negative alpha.
name: align*

accessible_name: Remaining sign cases for multiplying cuts
listen_text: Display. alpha times beta is defined in three remaining sign cases. If alpha and beta are both negative, use negative alpha times negative beta. If alpha is negative and beta is positive, take the negative of negative alpha times beta. If alpha is positive and beta is negative, take the negative of alpha times negative beta.
long_description: Three-row piecewise definition for negative factors.
name: align*

accessible_name: Eight commutative-ring laws
listen_text: Display. the eight commutative-ring laws: associativity of addition and multiplication; commutativity of addition and multiplication; additive identity zero; multiplicative identity one; existence of an additive inverse for each a; and distributivity of multiplication over addition.
long_description: Aligned table of associativity, commutativity, identities, additive inverse, and distributivity.
name: align*
source_block:
\begin{align*}
		\emph{Associativity}&&a + (b+ c) & = (a + b) + c \\
		&& (a \times b) \times c & = a \times (b\times c)\\
		\emph{Commutativity}&&a + b &= b+ a  \\
		&&  a \times b&= b\times a\\ 
		\emph{Identities}&&a + 0 &= a \\
		&& a \times 1 &= a\\
		\emph{Additive Inverse}&&(\exists b\in S)0&=a + b\\
		\emph{Distributivity}&&a \times (b+ c ) &= (a \times b) + (a \times c)
	\end{align*}

accessible_name: Definition of a commutative ring
listen_text: Definition. A commutative ring is a set S with distinguished elements zero and one and operations plus and times satisfying eight universally quantified laws over S: associativity of addition; associativity of multiplication; commutativity of addition; commutativity of multiplication; additive identity zero; multiplicative identity one; existence of an additive inverse for every a; and distributivity of multiplication over addition. The distinguished zero and one need not be the natural numbers with those names.
long_description: Defines a commutative ring by eight universally quantified algebraic laws.
name: defn
source_block:
\begin{defn}
	A \emph{commutative ring} is a set $S$, equipped with specific elements $0$ and $1$ and operations $+$ and $\times$, satisfying these eight formulas:
	\begin{align*}
		\emph{Associativity}&&a + (b+ c) & = (a + b) + c \\
		&& (a \times b) \times c & = a \times (b\times c)\\
		\emph{Commutativity}&&a + b &= b+ a  \\
		&&  a \times b&= b\times a\\ 
		\emph{Identities}&&a + 0 &= a \\
		&& a \times 1 &= a\\
		\emph{Additive Inverse}&&(\exists b\in S)0&=a + b\\
		\emph{Distributivity}&&a \times (b+ c ) &= (a \times b) + (a \times c)
	\end{align*}
	Implicitly, these are all bound with universal quantifiers restricted to $S$. And note that the elements $0$ and~$1$ here need not be the natural numbers with the same name.
\end{defn}

accessible_name: Associativity calculation for integer addition
listen_text: Display. seven-line associativity calculation. First, i plus the quantity j plus k equals the integer-equivalence class of a sub one comma b sub one, plus the sum of the classes of a sub two comma b sub two and a sub three comma b sub three. Second, combine the last two classes coordinatewise. Third, reassociate both natural-number coordinates. Fourth, use associativity of natural-number addition. Fifth, split the resulting class back into two classes. Sixth, identify those classes as i, j, and k. Seventh, the result is the quantity i plus j, plus k.
long_description: Seven aligned equalities proving i plus j plus k can be reassociated.
name: align*
source_block:
\begin{align*}
	i + (j + k) &= \equivrep{a_1, b_1}{}+(\equivrep{a_2, b_2}{} + \equivrep{a_3, b_3}{}) \\
	&= \equivrep{a_1,  b_1}{} + \equivrep{a_2+a_3, b_2+b_3}{}\\
	&= \equivrep{a_1 + (a_2 + a_3), b_1 + (b_2 + b_3)}{}\\
	&= \equivrep{(a_1 + a_2) + a_3, (b_1 + b_2) + b_3}{}\\
	&= \equivrep{a_1 + a_2, b_1 + b_2}{} + \equivrep{a_3, b_3}{}\\
	&= (\equivrep{a_1, b_1}{} + \equivrep{a_2, b_2}{}) + \equivrep{a_3, b_3}{}\\
	&= (i+j) + k
\end{align*}

accessible_name: Distributivity calculation for integer multiplication
listen_text: Display. seven-line distributivity calculation. Line one: i times open parenthesis j plus k close parenthesis equals the class of a sub one comma b sub one, times the sum of the classes of a sub two comma b sub two and a sub three comma b sub three. Line two: combine that sum coordinatewise. Line three: multiply the resulting classes, obtaining first coordinate a sub one times open parenthesis a sub two plus a sub three close parenthesis plus b sub one times open parenthesis b sub two plus b sub three close parenthesis, and second coordinate a sub one times open parenthesis b sub two plus b sub three close parenthesis plus b sub one times open parenthesis a sub two plus a sub three close parenthesis. Line four: after distribution, the first coordinate is a sub one times a sub two plus a sub one times a sub three plus b sub one times b sub two plus b sub one times b sub three, and the second coordinate is a sub one times b sub two plus a sub one times b sub three plus a sub two times b sub one plus a sub three times b sub one. Line five: split the class into the class with coordinates a sub one times a sub two plus b sub one times b sub two, and a sub one times b sub two plus a sub two times b sub one, plus the analogous class using subscript three. Line six: these are the product of i with j plus the product of i with k. Line seven: the result is i times j plus i times k.
long_description: Seven aligned equalities proving multiplication distributes over addition.
name: align*
source_block:
\begin{align*}
	i \times (j + k) 
	&= \equivrep{a_1, b_1}{} \times (\equivrep{a_2,b_2}{} + \equivrep{a_3, b_3}{})\\
	&= \equivrep{a_1, b_1}{} \times \equivrep{a_2 + a_3,b_2+b_3}{}\\
	&= \equivrep{a_1  (a_2 + a_3) + b_1  (b_2+b_3), a_1  (b_2 + b_3) + b_1 (a_2 + a_3)}{}\\
	&= \equivrep{a_1 a_2 + a_1a_3 + b_1 b_2+b_1b_3, a_1 b_2 + a_1b_3 + a_2b_1 + a_3b_1}{}\\		
%		&= \equivrep{a_1 a_2 + b_1b_2 + a_1a_3 + b_1 b_2+b_1b_3, a_1 b_2 + a_1b_3 + a_2b_1 + a_3b_1}{}\\		
	&= \equivrep{a_1a_2 + b_1b_2, a_1b_2 + a_2b_1}{} + \equivrep{a_1a_3 + b_1b_3, a_1b_3 + a_3b_1}{}\\
	&= (\equivrep{a_1, b_1}{} \times \equivrep{a_2,b_2}{}) + (\equivrep{a_1, b_1}{} \times  \equivrep{a_3, b_3}{})\\
	&= (i \times j) + (i \times k)
\end{align*}

accessible_name: Order compatibility laws for an ordered ring
listen_text: Display. two ordered-ring compatibility laws: if a is at most b, then a plus c is at most b plus c; and if a is at most b while c is nonnegative, then a times c is at most b times c.
long_description: Two implications expressing compatibility with addition and nonnegative multiplication.
name: align*

accessible_name: Definition of an ordered ring
listen_text: Definition. An ordered ring is a commutative ring equipped with a total order, less than or equal to, satisfying two compatibility laws. If a is at most b, then a plus c is at most b plus c. If a is at most b and c is nonnegative, then a times c is at most b times c.
long_description: An ordered ring is a commutative ring with a compatible total order.
name: defn

long_description: Every nonzero ring element has a multiplicative inverse.

accessible_name: Definition of an ordered field

accessible_name: Calculation proving p is less than q
listen_text: Display. four-line calculation proving p is less than q: p squared is less than two; p squared plus two times p is less than two plus two times p; p times open parenthesis p plus two close parenthesis is less than two plus two times p; therefore p is less than the fraction two plus two times p over p plus two, which equals q.
long_description: Four inequalities ending with p less than the defined rational q.
name: align*

accessible_name: Calculation proving q squared is less than two
listen_text: Display. six-line calculation proving q squared is less than two: p squared is less than two; two times p squared plus four times p plus two is less than p squared plus four times p plus four; four times p squared plus eight times p plus four is less than two times open parenthesis p squared plus four times p plus four close parenthesis; the square of the quantity two times p plus two is less than two times the square of the quantity p plus two; the square of the fraction with numerator two times p plus two and denominator p plus two is less than two; therefore q squared is less than two.
long_description: Six inequalities ending with q squared less than two.
name: align*

accessible_name: Definition of a Cauchy sequence
listen_text: Definition. A function f from the natural numbers to the rational numbers is a Cauchy sequence if and only if, for every positive rational epsilon, there is a natural-number index ell such that for all m and n greater than ell, the absolute value of f of m minus f of n is less than epsilon.
long_description: A rational-valued sequence is Cauchy when its values become arbitrarily close beyond some natural-number index.
name: defn

long_description: Unsolved exercise asking to show that zero and one over n-plus-one squared define real-equivalent Cauchy sequences.
name: prob

long_description: Two aligned definitions induced pointwise from representative sequences.

long_description: Two piecewise recursion clauses for f and g.
